title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

reading.body:
This is a case of an automated alert being treated as grounds for enforcement before anyone checked it. The failure sits at the point where a sensor reading becomes a police action: a license plate reader misread a single letter, produced a match to a similar vehicle, and the resulting alert was acted on as though it identified a stolen car. The man was detained at gunpoint for more than five minutes on the strength of that reading.

Catching it would have required independent verification of the alert before enforcement, which the vendor itself says should happen. The sheriff's office attributes the misread to an illegal tinted plate cover, which places the reading outside the conditions the reader was built to handle reliably. A degraded read and an unverified match are two separate gaps, and either one being closed would have broken the chain.

What is not established is that the plate cover caused the malfunction, which is the sheriff's account rather than a finding, and that the deputy's actions were reasonable, which is the office's own assessment of its own conduct.

reports.title: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover

summary: Steven Melvin, 42, of York County, South Carolina, was reportedly detained at gunpoint for more than five minutes after a Flock Safety license plate reader misread the first letter of his plate and matched his BMW to a similar stolen vehicle. The sheriff’s office later said an illegal tinted plate cover caused the malfunction, called the deputy’s actions reasonable, and Flock said alerts should be independently verified before enforcement.
title_en: York man was held at gunpoint over incorrect Flock hit. Sheriff blames illegal tag cover
